headings: Comparing the requirements across moral systems
Four proposed refutations and further tests
Two ten-question quizzes with final answers
Two sets of fifteen discussion questions
introHeading: What must a moral system establish?
intro: The original five prompts, the curator’s six proposed requirements and four proposed refutations are preserved in place. The two edited response tracks examine the demand for objective authority while distinguishing logical consistency, justification, access, responsibility and enforcement.
description: Assess moral systems through six proposed requirements, four challenges, comparisons, quizzes and discussion questions.
highlights: Consistency does not by itself establish moral authority.
A threat may motivate compliance without explaining why an obligation exists.
Tests of disagreement and unequal treatment must specify the system’s claims and hold relevant circumstances constant.

replacements.1.1.0: The six proposed elements test several different claims. A system can avoid contradiction yet fail to justify its authority, guide action or assign blame fairly. I will assess each requirement against the curator’s stronger target—morality that binds beyond social pressure—without assuming that all six are necessary for logical consistency alone.
replacements.1.1.1: Objective obligation: If a system claims duties that bind independently of approval, it must explain what makes them binding. Merely calling a rule “objective” supplies no explanation. A consistent conventional code can fail this authority test without contradicting itself; rejecting it as insufficiently moral therefore requires the stronger conception of morality stated in the prompt.
replacements.1.1.2: Punishment for immoral actions: Punishment can enforce a norm, but an obligation and a threat are different things. “You ought not betray a friend” does not become contradictory if the betrayal escapes punishment. Conversely, a powerful authority can punish conduct without establishing that it is wrong. The curator’s challenge therefore requires a further argument connecting genuine obligation with deserved or guaranteed punishment. Guilt is neither guaranteed nor a reliable measure of wrongdoing.
replacements.1.1.3: Access for all moral agents: A theory that blames people for violating unknowable requirements owes an account of fairness. Distinguish a rule’s truth, an agent’s opportunity to learn it and culpability for failing to do so. Unavoidable ignorance may excuse an agent even where a theory still judges the act wrong; deliberate avoidance of evidence is a different case.
replacements.1.1.4: Internal logical coherence: Under ordinary classical reasoning, a theory must not require and forbid the same action in the same circumstances and sense without explaining the conflict. Different initial duties need not contradict each other if the theory supplies priorities or distinguishes defeasible reasons from final obligations. Consistency is necessary for this standard of coherence, but a perfectly consistent rule can still be unsupported.
replacements.1.1.5: Distinguishable from emotions: Feeling abhorrence or compassion does not by itself establish the authority claimed for a judgment. Ask how the theory distinguishes warranted responses from prejudice or temporary mood. This preserves the curator’s demand for more than emotional assertion without assuming that every theory giving emotions a role is internally contradictory.
replacements.1.1.6: Moral autonomy: If a theory assigns responsibility, it must say what capacities and control make an agent answerable. That is not yet a proof that libertarian freedom—freedom incompatible with causal determination—is required. Compatibilists offer accounts of responsibility under determinism. The theory must defend its own account rather than move silently between these meanings of free will.
replacements.1.1.7: The strongest assessment keeps the tests separate: establish consistency, identify the claimed source of obligation, explain access and responsibility, and justify any sanctions. Passing the first test does not answer the curator’s central challenge about binding authority; failing to include punishment does not alone demonstrate contradiction.
replacements.1.2.0: The proposed requirements identify serious burdens for a theory claiming objective moral authority. Their logical status differs, however: some concern consistency, others justification, accountability or practical enforcement. Here is an assessment in the original order:
replacements.1.2.1: Objective obligation: Necessary for the particular claim that morality binds beyond convention or preference. It is not a logical prerequisite for every consistent ethical framework. An anti-realist must explain what force moral criticism retains; a realist must explain what makes the alleged objective demand authoritative. Neither can settle that dispute by definition alone.
replacements.1.2.3: Access for all moral agents: The demand is especially strong where the system assigns blame. Specify whether access means an opportunity for inquiry, reliable guidance or infallible knowledge. A person’s unavoidable inability to discover a requirement raises a culpability problem; it does not automatically show that the requirement is false.
replacements.1.2.4: Internal logical coherence: A system must avoid incompatible final requirements under the same conditions, or explain the logic by which it handles them. Arbitrariness and lack of justification are additional defects; neither is identical to formal contradiction.
replacements.1.2.5: Distinguishable from emotions: The curator’s challenge is how a feeling could warrant a demand on another person. A theory cannot answer simply by repeating that the feeling is intense. Sentimentalist theories may nevertheless provide standards for assessing emotions, so they require examination rather than dismissal as automatically incoherent.
replacements.1.2.6: Moral autonomy: Responsibility requires an account of agency and control. Whether that entails libertarian free will is contested; an account based on reasons-responsive action under determinism is a competing proposal, not a contradiction in terms.
replacements.1.2.7: I therefore retain the objection that punishment is not logically necessary, but withdraw the original blanket endorsement of libertarian freedom and objective obligation as conditions of consistency. Those are substantive commitments that must be defended. The curator’s stronger test remains: has the system earned the authority it claims over an agent?
replacements.2.1.0: These three systems address the proposed requirements in different ways. Their advocates’ answers are not demonstrations that every requirement has been satisfied. The following comparison keeps the six headings and notes where a theory rejects, qualifies or leaves a burden unresolved.
replacements.2.1.2: Objective obligation: Kant grounds duty in rational self-legislation and the categorical imperative, including the test of whether one can will a maxim as universal law. This is his proposed foundation of authority; stating the formula does not settle objections to its derivation or application.
replacements.2.1.3: Punishment: Contrary to the original response, Kant gives a substantial account of criminal punishment. In the Doctrine of Right, section on punishment, guilt for a crime is required; punishment cannot be imposed merely to produce benefits. This juridical account does not mean every ethical lapse must receive a legal penalty.
replacements.2.1.4: Access: Kant presents moral law as available to rational agency, not dependent on specialist revelation. Applying principles to uncertain circumstances still requires judgment; this claim does not establish that every agent reaches every correct verdict.
replacements.2.1.6: Distinguishable from emotions: Duty’s authority does not depend on whether we feel inclined to comply. Acting from duty need not involve suppressing every sympathetic feeling; the issue is what grounds the maxim and its moral worth.
replacements.2.1.9: Objective obligation: Classical utilitarianism evaluates conduct by its contribution to overall happiness, impartially considered. Maximizing aggregate welfare is not simply maximizing the number of beneficiaries. The principle supplies a criterion once accepted; why anyone is bound by it remains a justificatory question.
replacements.2.1.14: Moral autonomy: Agents deliberate about consequences, but their freedom of choice is not automatically an overriding constraint on welfare maximization. A utilitarian must explain the protection given to liberty and how conflicts with aggregate benefit are handled.
replacements.2.1.16: Objective obligation: Aristotelian virtue ethics connects virtues with human flourishing. Calling traits virtues does not establish that they are objectively good or translate every virtue into a categorical duty; the account of flourishing must be defended.
replacements.2.1.19: Internal coherence: Accepting that virtues contribute to a good life is not sufficient to prove consistency. The theory must explain how practical wisdom handles tensions among courage, justice, loyalty and other virtues.
replacements.2.1.20: Distinguishable from emotions: In Aristotle’s Nicomachean Ethics, Book II, virtue involves feeling and acting appropriately. Emotions are trained and assessed, not excluded. The challenge is to justify the standards of appropriateness.
replacements.2.1.21: Moral autonomy: Deliberate choice and practical wisdom matter, but Aristotle’s account should not be equated with Kantian self-legislation. Habituation and education shape an agent’s ability to choose well.
replacements.2.2.0: The following four approaches can be compared against the curator’s six requirements. Their proposed foundations remain contestable. The original response omitted punishment from each comparison; that missing criterion is now addressed within each entry.
replacements.2.2.2:
Objective obligation: Divine command theories ground duties in divine commands. Whether obedience is owed, and whether the commands are arbitrary, remain questions to answer; not every religious ethic is a divine command theory.
Punishment: Some religious accounts add divine sanctions, but commands and punishment are conceptually distinct. Threats alone would establish an incentive, not moral authority.
replacements.2.2.3: Access: Proposed routes include revelation, scripture and reason. Unequal exposure, conflicting revelations and interpretive disagreement must be addressed before universal accessibility is established.
replacements.2.2.4: Logical coherence: A perfect, non-contradictory divine source would be relevant if established, but attributing perfection does not resolve apparent conflicts among the commands that humans actually claim to receive.
replacements.2.2.6: Moral autonomy: Choosing whether to obey can count as agency, but obedience to another will is not the same as Kantian autonomy. The account must explain freedom and responsibility on its own terms.
replacements.2.2.8:
Objective obligation: Kant proposes that the categorical imperative expresses rational duty.
Punishment: His juridical account grounds punishment in criminal guilt, rather than utility alone; see the linked primary text in the preceding response. Not every breach of ethical duty is thereby a crime.
replacements.2.2.14:
Objective obligation: Aristotelian ethics connects virtue to eudaimonia, or human flourishing. This offers a proposed standard of good activity, not a simple catalogue of obligatory commands.
Punishment: Moral education and habituation are central; a virtue-based approach can assess correction by justice and character formation without making guaranteed punishment a condition of every moral judgment.
replacements.2.2.17: Distinguishable from emotions: Properly educated emotions are part of virtue, alongside practical wisdom. A feeling’s intensity does not establish its appropriateness.
replacements.2.2.20:
Objective obligation: Classical utilitarianism directs impartial promotion of overall happiness or well-being. Its authority still needs justification.
Punishment: Consequences such as prevention and rehabilitation must justify the suffering imposed. Mill also examines internal and external motives for compliance in Utilitarianism, Chapter III; motivation should not be confused with proving a moral principle.
replacements.2.2.24: Moral autonomy: Agents can reason about effects, but that capacity is different from treating each person’s choices as inviolable. Utilitarian accounts must explain when liberty constrains action or is protected because of its consequences.
replacements.2.2.25: These are proposed answers, not certificates of coherence or objectivity. They differ over whether punishment is fundamental, what access requires and what autonomy means. The curator’s comparison is most useful when each system must state and defend its answer to every requirement instead of receiving credit merely for using the same vocabulary.
replacements.3.1.0: Each proposed refutation targets a claim worth testing. The key is to distinguish contradiction in the principles from failure in application, and to compare cases with the same morally relevant features. Here are the four challenges and additional criteria in their original order:
replacements.3.1.2: Elaboration: Disagreement puts pressure on a claim of clear, universal access, especially among careful, equally informed agents. Access alone, however, does not imply infallibility: people can have access to arithmetic and still make mistakes. Disagreement therefore needs an argument linking it to the theory’s specific accessibility claim.
replacements.3.1.3: Evaluative criteria: Identify the exact disputed proposition, equalize factual information where possible, and ask what procedure the system supplies to resolve the dispute. If it promises certain agreement under those conditions, persistent disagreement is a direct problem. Otherwise it may indicate weak guidance or justification rather than logical contradiction.
replacements.3.1.5: Elaboration: The slavery example challenges a theory that changes its verdict merely because an era changes while the relevant coercion and harms remain the same. Distinguish a change in moral truth from a change in people’s recognition of it. A population’s former approval does not show that slavery was then justified.
replacements.3.1.6: Evaluative criteria: Compare the same action under the same relevant conditions. Demand an explanation of any claimed difference and test it independently of the desired verdict. New information may correct an earlier judgment; “it was accepted then” alone does not answer the curator’s objection.
replacements.3.1.8: Elaboration: If the same treatment is condemned for Group A but permitted for Group B solely because of group identity, a theory claiming impartial authority owes a justification. Different practical rules can nevertheless follow from one principle where relevant circumstances differ.
replacements.3.1.9: Evaluative criteria: Swap group labels while holding coercion, interests and other relevant facts fixed. If the verdict changes, require a reason that does not merely repeat the favored group’s status. Do not let an appeal to “culture” conceal the same exploitation the theory condemns elsewhere.
replacements.3.1.11: Elaboration: Unequal punishment for relevantly equivalent offenses challenges a system’s claim to equal justice. Distinguish what the theory requires from what officials actually do: corrupt enforcement can violate a coherent rule rather than reveal a contradiction within it.
replacements.3.1.12: Evaluative criteria: Compare culpability, intent, knowledge, coercion and harm, then ask whether the stated rationale explains the difference. A theory must also justify punishment itself. Harm alone cannot determine every penalty: an accident and an intentional attack can cause equal damage while differing in responsibility.
replacements.3.1.17: These tests assess different strengths. Contradictory requirements, unsupported authority, inaccessible guidance and unfair enforcement are serious but distinct defects. A precise critique states which defect has been shown and what further claim remains unproved.
replacements.3.2.0: The four challenges can expose weaknesses, but none should be treated as an automatic refutation without specifying the theory’s claims and the circumstances being compared.
replacements.3.2.1: Disagreement on moral facts: Persistent informed disagreement may undermine claims of easy or reliable access. It does not by itself establish that no truth exists. Ask what access was promised, whether the disputants satisfy its conditions and how the theory diagnoses error without simply favoring its supporters.
replacements.3.2.2: Temporal inconsistency: A theory cannot defend slavery merely by pointing to its historical acceptance while claiming standards independent of acceptance. Hold relevant features fixed and distinguish moral truth from past belief about it. Changing knowledge can explain corrected verdicts without proving that truth itself changed.
replacements.3.2.3: Regional inconsistency: Demand the same treatment of relevantly equivalent cases. Regional differences in circumstances can matter; the label of the region alone supplies no justification. A theory openly relativizing morality may be coherent yet fail the curator’s stronger requirement of objective authority.
replacements.3.2.4: Inconsistent punishments: Compare cases with equivalent culpability and relevant circumstances, and distinguish the rule from its enforcement. A difference may reveal partiality, an undisclosed criterion or abuse. Determine which before declaring the underlying principles contradictory.
replacements.3.2.6: Handling moral dilemmas: Ask how conflicting reasons relate to final obligations. A theory may offer priority rules, permit several choices or acknowledge a genuine dilemma. Failure to give a unique answer is a limitation of guidance, not automatically a contradiction.
replacements.3.2.7: Justifying foundations: Require reasons for basic premises and for their claimed authority. An arbitrary foundation can be consistent; this criterion therefore tests justification as well as coherence.
replacements.3.2.9: The result should be a diagnosis: what contradicts what, which claim lacks support, and which agents cannot apply the rule? This keeps the curator’s challenge sharp while avoiding the mistaken inference that every practical difficulty proves a logical inconsistency.
replacements.4.1.3: How does Kant’s account of criminal punishment differ from a purely utilitarian justification?
replacements.4.1.13: They purport to bind independently of social pressure or personal approval. Their existence and authority still require justification.
replacements.4.1.14: Kant requires criminal guilt and rejects using punishment merely to produce benefits; a utilitarian justification assesses the consequences of imposing it.
replacements.4.1.17: It matters especially to fair blame: a system must distinguish unavoidable ignorance from culpable failure to learn. Accessibility alone does not guarantee correct judgment.
replacements.4.1.18: It grounds duty in rational principles rather than inclination; this does not require the absence of every sympathetic feeling.
replacements.4.1.20: It challenges changes of verdict based merely on the era while relevant facts remain fixed. Changes in belief or information need not be changes in moral truth.
replacements.4.1.21: Unjustified differences between relevantly equivalent cases challenge universal authority; differences supported by relevant circumstances need not do so.
replacements.4.1.22: A justified rationale, proportionality, and consistent treatment of equivalent cases, including intent, knowledge, coercion and harm—not harm alone.
replacements.4.2.1: Which proposed element is challenged as unnecessary for internal consistency because enforcement and obligation are different questions?
replacements.4.2.5: What criterion does classical utilitarianism propose for judging actions?
replacements.4.2.6: Does access to moral inquiry logically guarantee agreement on every moral judgment? Explain.
replacements.4.2.7: What must be held fixed when comparing moral verdicts across different times?
replacements.4.2.8: When would a regional difference in verdict challenge a system’s claim to impartial authority?
replacements.4.2.9: What should a theory explain when moral reasons pull toward incompatible actions?
replacements.4.2.10: Why should a theory’s foundations be tested for justification as well as consistency?
replacements.4.2.17: No. Access need not imply infallibility. Persistent informed disagreement nevertheless puts pressure on a theory’s specific claims about reliable or certain access.
replacements.4.2.18: The relevant features of the act and circumstances; distinguish changes in belief from changes in truth.
replacements.4.2.19: When relevantly equivalent cases receive different verdicts without a justified difference beyond group or regional identity.
replacements.4.2.20: How competing reasons relate to final obligations: through priorities, permitted alternatives or an acknowledged dilemma.
replacements.4.2.21: A consistent set of premises can still be arbitrary or unsupported; consistency alone does not establish binding authority.

responseDecisions.1.1: Assess all six exact curator requirements; distinguish logical necessity from objective authority, access, blame and enforcement.
responseDecisions.1.2: Retain punishment objection; correct unsupported blanket necessity claims for objective duties and libertarian free will.
responseDecisions.2.1: Retain three systems and six criteria each; correct Kant punishment, utility formula, autonomy and virtue coherence.
responseDecisions.2.2: Retain four systems and original criterion order; supply omitted punishment treatment within each first criterion and qualify claimed objectivity.
responseDecisions.3.1: Retain four refutations and three additional criteria; test same circumstances, distinguish recognition/truth and rule/enforcement.
responseDecisions.3.2: Retain four challenges and three criteria; clarify access/agreement, contextual application, dilemmas and justification.
responseDecisions.4.1: Retain ten questions/end key; correct Kant item and answers dependent on qualified criteria.
responseDecisions.4.2: Retain ten questions/end key; repair missing-options first item and overstrong disagreement/time/region answers.
